name: Grigori Chukhrai
teaser: Soviet director whose Ballad of a Soldier turned a war story into an aching human poem about one soldier's journey home.

exploreAction.targetName: Ballad of a Soldier (1959) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a soldier's six days of leave become an epic. Chukhrai films war's cost in quiet, human gestures.

name: Marlen Khutsiev
teaser: Soviet director of I Am Twenty, a moody portrait of Moscow youth that captured the 1960s thaw better than any official film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the city itself — streets, trams, parties — as the real character. Khutsiev films a generation drifting without a map.

name: Georgiy Daneliya
teaser: Soviet director of warm, wry comedies and the cosmic satire Kin-dza-dza!, beloved for finding tenderness in absurdity.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a small-town pilot chase his dream to Moscow. Daneliya makes gentle comedy out of the gap between languages and lives.

name: Eldar Ryazanov
teaser: Soviet master of the romantic comedy whose New Year's classic The Irony of Fate is still broadcast every January 1 across Russia.

exploreAction.targetName: The Irony of Fate (1975) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a drunk man ends up in the wrong city, in the wrong apartment, with the wrong woman. Ryazanov builds farce on Soviet urban uniformity.

name: Vladimir Menshov
teaser: Soviet director of Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears, the Oscar-winning saga of three women chasing love and careers across two decades.

exploreAction.targetName: Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the film jumps between 1958 and 1979. Menshov films a whole generation's bargains with fate.

name: Karen Shakhnazarov
teaser: Armenian-Russian director who mixed Soviet surrealism and satire — his Courier catches a teenager's rebellion against the system's boredom.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a slacker who talks his way through a dead-end job. Shakhnazarov films youthful irony against a crumbling system.

name: Gleb Panfilov
teaser: Soviet director who made fierce films about women and power, built around his wife, the great actress Inna Churikova.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a writer confront his own mediocrity in a provincial town. Panfilov films conscience as an argument with yourself.

name: Andrei Zvyagintsev
teaser: Russian director of austere, biblical-scale dramas about faith and corruption — Leviathan put a whole country on trial.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the landscape — sea, whale bones, gray sky — loom over the characters. Zvyagintsev films power as weather.

name: Pavel Lungin
teaser: Russian-French director whose Taxi Blues captured perestroika's chaos — a puritan saxophonist and a thuggish taxi driver forced together.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two men who despise each other become roommates. Lungin films the Soviet collapse as a buddy comedy with bruises.

name: Yuli Raizman
teaser: Soviet director of The Communist, a portrait of the revolution's builders that both flattered and quietly mourned the system.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how one man's devotion outruns the machinery he serves. Raizman films idealism with a knowing sadness.

name: Sergei Bondarchuk
teaser: Soviet director and actor whose War and Peace remains the most expensive, most gigantic single film ever attempted — 600 extras per shot.

exploreAction.targetName: War and Peace (1966) — the battle of Borodino sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the sheer scale — circling cameras, thousands of extras, and one woman's face in the middle of it all.

name: Aleksandr Ptushko
teaser: Soviet fantasy pioneer who filled the screen with giants, dragons, and magic — the Walt Disney of the East, if Disney were a bureaucrat.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the mid-century special effects with awe, not irony. Ptushko staged a whole myth with puppets, miniatures, and will.

name: Ivan Pyryev
teaser: Soviet director of operatic kolkhoz musicals — singing tractor drivers and dancing harvests — that Stalin loved and cinephiles still debate.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cossacks of the Kuban (1949) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the spectacle with fresh eyes: choreographed wheat, brass bands, and propaganda dressed as joy.

name: Yakov Protazanov
teaser: Russian pioneer who made Aelita, the 1924 science-fiction epic of a Martian civilization — Soviet cinema's first space trip.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Constructivist Martian sets — triangles, geometry, and revolution in space. Protazanov made history look futuristic.

name: Aleksandr Dovzhenko
teaser: Ukrainian poet of Soviet cinema whose Earth turned the harvest into a luminous national elegy about death, grain, and renewal.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a man's death and the wheat that grows after it become the same image. Dovzhenko films a whole world in faces and fruit.

name: Sergei Gerasimov
teaser: Soviet director and teacher who trained generations of Russian filmmakers and made the epic And Quiet Flows the Don.

exploreAction.targetName: And Quiet Flows the Don (1957) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the river and the steppe frame a family's tragedy. Gerasimov films Tolstoy's scope with a village's intimacy.

name: Mikhail Romm
teaser: Soviet director of Nine Days of One Year, the atomic-scientist drama that made physics look like the most romantic job on Earth.

exploreAction.targetName: Nine Days of One Year (1962) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch two physicists argue about safety, love, and progress over cigarettes. Romm films intellect as heroism.

name: Alexander Askoldov
teaser: Soviet director whose one film, Commissar, was banned for twenty years — a harrowing story of a Red Army woman and a Jewish family.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a soldier's hardness cracks against a family's warmth. Askoldov films ideology meeting humanity head-on.

name: Vladimir Motyl
teaser: Soviet director of White Sun of the Desert, the beloved desert western cosmonauts watched before every launch.

exploreAction.targetName: White Sun of the Desert (1970) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a Red Army soldier escort a harem across the desert. Motyl mixes action, humor, and folk-song melancholy into a genre all its own.

name: Leonid Gaidai
teaser: Soviet comedy genius whose slapstick masterpieces — Operation Y, The Diamond Arm — are quoted by every Russian speaker to this day.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch three comic shorts with vaudeville timing. Gaidai found comedy in queues, bureaucracy, and one very persistent trio of idiots.

name: Károly Makk
teaser: Hungarian director of Love, a two-woman chamber piece about memory and loyalty that slipped one of the era's most radical films past censors.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch a mother and daughter-in-law orbit a lie they both maintain. Makk films kindness as a form of resistance.

name: Márta Mészáros
teaser: Hungarian director of Adoption, the first Hungarian film by a woman, and a lifelong chronicler of mothers, daughters, and the gaps between them.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch two women from different generations talk honestly about children and choice. Mészáros films intimacy without decoration.

name: Ildikó Enyedi
teaser: Hungarian director of On Body and Soul, the dreamy Oscar-nominated romance between two colleagues who discover they share the same dreams.

exploreAction.targetName: On Body and Soul (2017) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the deer dream sequences. Enyedi films two loners finding each other in a place where words don't reach.

name: László Nemes
teaser: Hungarian director of Son of Saul, the Holocaust film that refuses to look away — shot in tight close-up with the horror always just out of frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Son of Saul (2015) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the shallow focus traps you with Saul. Nemes makes the off-screen space the source of dread.

name: Kornél Mundruczó
teaser: Hungarian director of volatile, confrontational dramas — his White God turned Budapest's stray dogs into an army of reckoning.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the dogs take over the city. Mundruczó films an uprising that is also a metaphor, and lets both be real.

name: Zoltán Fábri
teaser: Hungarian director of literary adaptations and stark war dramas, twice nominated for the Oscar for films about conscience and complicity.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fifth Seal (1976) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch five men argue about heroism in a shop at night. Fábri turns philosophy into a thriller about who will break first.

name: Péter Bacsó
teaser: Hungarian director of The Witness, a satirical masterpiece banned for twelve years — a fruit inspector who accidentally becomes a leader.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the absurdist rise of a small man in a big system. Bacsó's satire was so sharp the state shelved it for over a decade.

name: András Kovács
teaser: Hungarian director of Cold Days, the postwar reckoning film that asked a town to remember what its people did in the war.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch four men reconstruct a massacre from memory, each version shifting blame. Kovács films history as an argument without an ending.

name: György Fehér
teaser: Hungarian minimalist who, with filmmaker-composer Mihály Vig, made bleak, trance-like films of crime and punishment in grainy black and white.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the fixed, patient camera and the repeating music. Fehér turns a murder plot into a slow ritual of doom.

name: Gyula Gazdag
teaser: Hungarian director of inventive satires and later a beloved teacher of American indie filmmaking at UCLA.

exploreAction.targetName: The Whistling Cobblestone (1972) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a young worker's absurd odyssey through bureaucracy. Gazdag films the system as a maze with no exit and lots of doors.

name: Ferenc Kósa
teaser: Hungarian director of The Upthrown Stone, a lyrical family saga spanning three generations of a Hungarian village.

exploreAction.targetName: The Upthrown Stone (1969) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a family's history is told through a boy's eyes. Kósa films the land and the men who work it as one story.

name: Péter Gothár
teaser: Hungarian director of Time Stands Still, a generation portrait of teenagers coming of age inside the hushed late-1950s.

exploreAction.targetName: Time Stands Still (1982) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch a boarding school become a pressure cooker of secret songs and stolen radios. Gothár films adolescence as historical memory.

name: Gábor Bódy
teaser: Hungarian avant-garde theorist and filmmaker whose dense, encyclopedic films merged philosophy, video art, and cinema — he died at 39.

exploreAction.targetName: Narcissus and Psyche (1980) — the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Let the collage of film stocks and eras wash over you. Bódy was building a cinema of ideas, not stories.

name: Zsolt Kézdi-Kovács
teaser: Hungarian director of Forbidden Relations, a blunt rural drama about a sister and brother who fall in love and face a village's judgment.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the village reacts before the couple does. Kézdi-Kovács films taboo as a social, not private, event.

name: Ágnes Kocsis
teaser: Hungarian director of quiet observational dramas — her Fresh Air follows a teenage girl whose father returns to a home that moved on.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the everyday details — smoking, working, eating — that make up a girl's world. Kocsis films absence without melodrama.

name: Szabolcs Hajdu
teaser: Hungarian director of loose, ensemble family dramas — his Bibliothèque Pascal mixed social realism with Kafkaesque fantasy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how a fairy tale and a trafficking story occupy the same film. Hajdu refuses to separate fantasy from cruelty.

name: Nimród Antal
teaser: Hungarian-American director who moved from Budapest crime thrillers to Hollywood survival horror — a genre craftsman with a feel for pressure.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch subway ticket inspectors hunt a mysterious pusher. Antal films a subterranean Budapest with deadpan style and real menace.

name: György Pálfi
teaser: Hungarian formalist of Taxidermia — a century-spanning triptych of gluttony, sex, and taxidermy told with baroque, absurdist invention.

exploreAction.instruction: Expect the grotesque to be beautiful. Pálfi films appetite as history — from a soldier's fantasy to a man who stuffs animals.

name: Benedek Fliegauf
teaser: Hungarian director of hypnotic, wordless dramas and the climate-myth allegory Womb — cinema as atmosphere first, story second.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how style replaces plot — long shots, loud music, a man drifting through a Budapest of low deals. Fliegauf films trance states.

name: István Gaál
teaser: Hungarian director of The Falcons, a spare, brooding fable of an aging falconer and a young rebel on the Hungarian plains.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the birds and the men who carry them. Gaál films a vanishing way of life with mournful precision.
